story.e: In Caesarea lived a Roman centurion named Cornelius. He was a soldier, an officer of the occupying army — exactly the kind of man a Jewish family would not have invited to dinner. Yet the book writes this about him: he was a devout man who feared God with his whole household, gave generously to the poor and prayed to God continually. One afternoon he saw an angel in a vision who called him by name and said: your prayers and your giving have come up before God. Send to Joppa and call for Simon Peter, who is staying with a tanner by the sea. Cornelius sent three men at once. The next day, as they were approaching the city, Peter went up on the roof to pray. He became hungry, and while the food was being prepared he saw a vision: heaven opened and something like a large sheet came down, full of all kinds of animals — including ones the law called unclean, which a Jew would never eat. And a voice said: “Get up, Peter, kill and eat!” Peter objected: “By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten anything unclean.” The voice spoke a second time: “What God has made clean, do not call unclean!” This happened three times, and then the sheet was taken up. Peter was puzzled about what it could mean. Just then Cornelius’s men arrived, and the Spirit said: go with them, for I have sent them. So Peter set out. The next day they reached Caesarea, where Cornelius had gathered his relatives and close friends. Peter stepped into the house of a Gentile — something he had always strictly avoided — and said: “You know it is forbidden for a Jew to associate with someone of another nation. But God has shown me that I should call no one unholy.” Then he began to speak about Jesus. And while he was still speaking, the Holy Spirit came down on all who were listening. The believers who had come with Peter were astonished: the Spirit had been poured out on Gentiles too. Peter asked: can anyone refuse them the water? And he baptised them. This part is the book’s greatest turning point. It is not that one man was converted in it, but that a boundary disappeared.
story.m: In Caesarea lived a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was called the Italian cohort. He was a Roman officer in the occupying army — exactly the kind of man a Jerusalem Jewish family would not have invited over for supper. Yet the book writes this about him: he was devout, he feared God with his whole household, he gave generously to the people and prayed to God continually. About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in to him and call him by name. Alarmed, Cornelius asked: “What is it, Lord?” The angel answered: “Your prayers and your gifts to the poor have come up before God, and he has remembered you. Now send men to Joppa and call for Simon, who is called Peter. He is staying in the house of a tanner named Simon, by the sea.” When the angel had gone, Cornelius called two servants and a devout soldier, told them everything and sent them to Joppa. The next day, as they were approaching the city, Peter went up on the roof to pray, about the sixth hour. Meanwhile he grew hungry and wanted to eat. While the food was being prepared, he fell into a trance: he saw heaven opened and something like a large sheet coming down, lowered by its four corners to the ground. In it were all kinds of four-footed animals, reptiles and birds — among them creatures the law called unclean, which a God-fearing Jew would never have touched. And a voice said to him: “Get up, Peter, kill and eat!” But Peter replied: “By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten anything unholy or unclean.” The voice spoke a second time: “What God has made clean, do not call unclean!” This happened three times, and then the sheet was at once taken up into heaven. Peter was completely at a loss, wondering what the vision could mean. Just then Cornelius’s men arrived and were asking at the gate for Peter. And the Spirit said to him: “Look, three men are looking for you. Get up, go down and go with them! Do not hesitate, for I have sent them.” So Peter went down, welcomed them, and the next day set out with them. The day after that they reached Caesarea, where Cornelius was waiting and had gathered his relatives and close friends. When Peter came in, Cornelius met him and fell at his feet, but Peter raised him: “Stand up, I am only a man myself!” Then he stepped into the house — and that step alone was a greater act than anything he had said before. He told them: “You know that it is forbidden for a Jew to associate with a foreigner or to enter his house. But God has shown me that I should call no one unholy or unclean.” Cornelius told him his vision, and Peter began his speech: “Now I truly understand that God is not one to show favouritism, but in every nation the one who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him.” He spoke to them about Jesus, the crucifixion and the resurrection. And while he was still speaking, the Holy Spirit came down on all who were listening to the word. The Jewish believers who had come with Peter were amazed that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out on Gentiles too. Then Peter asked: “Can anyone refuse the water for baptising these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we did?” And he ordered them to be baptised. This part is the book’s greatest turning point. It is not that one man was converted in it, but that a boundary disappeared which until then everyone had taken for granted.
story.h: This chapter is the longest continuous scene in Acts, and not by accident. Let us look at eight things. The first is whom it is about. Cornelius is a Roman centurion: an officer of the occupying army, in everyday speech the enemy. Yet the writer says four things about him before anything happens: devout, God-fearing, generous, praying. This removes an objection in advance: no one can say “he was just a pagan soldier”. The second is the double vision. Cornelius gets one and Peter gets one. That structure matters: the story does not work by a believer going to an unbeliever. Something is needed on both sides for the meeting to happen. The third is Peter’s refusal, which is not disobedience but loyalty. All his life he took seriously what he had learned from God, and now he is asked to cross exactly that. “By no means, Lord” is a self-contradictory sentence, and the text does not smooth it over. The fourth is the threefold repetition. Not three times because Peter is deaf, but because this kind of change does not fit into one sentence. Earlier in the book he was made to say something three times too — by the lake, after the resurrection. Luke, the writer, knows this. The fifth is that the vision is not about what it seems. It speaks of food, but Peter himself states its meaning: “that I should call no one unholy”. Behind the rules stood people. The sixth is the sentence that is one of the book’s axes: “God is not one to show favouritism.” Peter does not say he always knew this. He says: now I understand. An experience taught him, not an argument. The seventh is the order of events, which overturns the usual. Normally teaching comes, then a decision, then the Spirit. Here the Spirit comes down before Peter has finished — and so God settles a question people have not even debated yet. In the next chapter Peter will have to defend this in Jerusalem, and his only argument will be that he could not prevent it. The eighth is the wider context. So far the book has advanced step by step: Jerusalem, Samaria, an Ethiopian traveller. But all of those were connected to the people in some way. Cornelius is not. From here on Christianity is no longer one nation’s internal affair. That decision was not made at a council but in a dining room in Caesarea.

verse.text: God is not one to show favouritism.

story.e: A hír gyorsabban ért Jeruzsálembe, mint Péter. Meghallották az apostolok és a testvérek Júdeában, hogy a pogányok is befogadták Isten igéjét. És amikor Péter visszaérkezett, nem gratuláltak neki. Számon kérték: „Pogány emberekhez mentél be, és együtt ettél velük!” Érdemes megállni ennél. Nem a tanítást kifogásolták, nem azt, hogy Jézusról beszélt. Az étkezést. Hogy leült az asztalukhoz. Mert ez volt az a pont, ahol a két világ összeért, és ahol a határ a leginkább látszott. Péter pedig nem vitatkozott, és nem is védekezett elvekkel. Elkezdte elmondani, sorjában, hogy mi történt. Elmondta a látomást a lepedőről, a hangot, a saját tiltakozását, a háromszori ismétlést. Elmondta, hogy közben megérkeztek a küldöttek, és hogy a Lélek azt mondta: menj el velük, semmit ne tétovázz. Elmondta, hogy hatan vele tartottak — vagyis vannak tanúi. És elmondta a lényeget: amikor beszélni kezdett, a Szentlélek leszállt rájuk, éppúgy, ahogy rájuk kezdetben. Majd hozzátette azt a mondatot, amely a rész szíve: „Ha tehát ugyanazt az ajándékot adta nekik Isten, mint nekünk, akik hittünk az Úr Jézus Krisztusban, akkor ki vagyok én, hogy akadályozzam Istent?” Péter tehát nem azt mondja, hogy neki igaza volt. Azt mondja: nem tudtam megakadályozni, és nem is lett volna jogom hozzá. Amikor ezt hallották, elcsendesedtek. Aztán dicsőíteni kezdték Istent, és azt mondták: „Eszerint a pogányoknak is megadta Isten a megtérést az életre.” Ez a néhány mondat a Biblia egyik legszebb jelenete. Egy közösség, amely valamit egész életében biztosan tudott, meghallgat egy beszámolót — és meggondolja magát. Nem azért, mert legyőzték vitában, hanem mert valami megtörtént, amit nem lehetett másképp magyarázni. És érdemes észrevenni a szavakat is: nem azt mondják, hogy „rendben, kivételt teszünk”. Azt mondják, hogy Isten adta nekik is. Vagyis nem engedményt tesznek, hanem felismernek valamit.
story.m: A hír gyorsabban ért Jeruzsálembe, mint Péter. Meghallották az apostolok és a Júdeában élő testvérek, hogy a pogányok is befogadták Isten igéjét. És amikor Péter felment Jeruzsálembe, nem gratuláltak neki: vitatkozni kezdtek vele a körülmetéltek közül valók. A vád így hangzott: „Pogány emberekhez mentél be, és együtt ettél velük.” Érdemes megállni ennél a mondatnál, mert pontosan mutatja, hol volt a határ. Nem azt kifogásolták, hogy Péter Jézusról beszélt nekik, és nem is azt, hogy megkeresztelte őket. Az étkezést. Azt, hogy leült egy pogány ember asztalához, és onnan evett. Az asztal volt az a hely, ahol a két világ ténylegesen összeért, és ahol a legnehezebb volt átlépni. Péter azonban nem vitatkozott, és nem is elvekkel védekezett. Belefogott, és sorjában elbeszélte nekik az egészet. Elmondta, hogy Joppéban imádkozott, és révületben látomást látott: egy nagy lepedőhöz hasonló edény ereszkedett le négy sarkánál fogva, tele négylábú állatokkal, vadakkal, csúszómászókkal és madarakkal. Elmondta, hogy hangot hallott: „Kelj fel, Péter, öld és egyél!” És hogy ő ezt felelte: „Semmiképpen sem, Uram, mert szentségtelen vagy tisztátalan soha nem ment a számba.” Elmondta, hogy a hang másodszor is szólt: „Amit Isten megtisztított, azt te ne mondd tisztátalannak!” És hogy ez háromszor történt meg, majd minden felemelkedett az égbe. Elmondta, hogy ebben a pillanatban érkezett meg a három férfi Cezáreából, és hogy a Lélek azt mondta neki: menjen el velük, semmit ne tétovázzon. Hozzátette azt is, hogy hat testvér vele együtt elment — vagyis nem egyedül mesél, hanem tanúkkal. Aztán elmondta, mi történt a házban: Kornéliusz elbeszélte a saját látomását, és amikor Péter beszélni kezdett, a Szentlélek leszállt rájuk, ugyanúgy, ahogy rájuk a kezdetben. És ekkor mondta ki azt, ami a rész szíve: „Ha tehát ugyanazt az ajándékot adta nekik Isten, mint nekünk, akik hittünk az Úr Jézus Krisztusban, akkor ki vagyok én, hogy akadályozzam Istent?” Péter tehát nem azt állítja, hogy neki volt igaza. Azt mondja: nem tudtam megakadályozni, és nem is lett volna jogom hozzá. Amikor mindezt hallották, megnyugodtak, és dicsőítették Istent ezekkel a szavakkal: „Eszerint a pogányoknak is megadta Isten a megtérést az életre.” Ez a néhány mondat a Biblia egyik legszebb jelenete. Egy közösség, amely valamit egész életében biztosan tudott, meghallgat egy beszámolót — és meggondolja magát. Nem azért, mert legyőzték vitában, hanem mert valami megtörtént, amit nem lehetett másképp magyarázni. És érdemes figyelni a szavaikra is: nem azt mondják, hogy „rendben, tegyünk kivételt”. Azt mondják, hogy Isten adta meg nekik is. Nem engedményt tesznek, hanem felismernek valamit, ami már megtörtént.
story.h: Ez a rész első olvasásra ismétlés: Péter elmondja még egyszer, amit az előző fejezetben már olvastunk. De a megismétlés itt a lényeg. Nyolc dolgot nézzünk meg. Az első a vád pontos szövege. Nem az a kifogás, hogy Péter tanított pogányoknak, és nem is az, hogy megkeresztelte őket. „Együtt ettél velük.” Az asztal volt a valódi határ. Könnyebb elfogadni valakit elvben, mint leülni mellé enni; a könyv pontosan tudja, melyik a nehezebb. A második, hogy Péter mit nem csinál. Nem hivatkozik a tekintélyére, pedig megtehetné: ő az első a tizenkettő között. Nem idéz írást, és nem érvel elvekkel. Elmeséli, mi történt. A harmadik a tanúk említése. „Velem jött ez a hat testvér is.” Péter nem a saját élményére épít, hanem olyasmire, amit mások is láttak. Ez a mondat teszi a beszámolót ellenőrizhetővé, és ezért van ott. A negyedik a sorrend, amelyet Péter követ: a saját tiltakozásával kezdi. Elmondja, hogy ő maga is nemet mondott, méghozzá kétszer. Ezzel nem fölé kerül a hallgatóinak, hanem mellé: én is pontosan ezt gondoltam. Ez a meggyőzés egyik legrégebbi és legtisztességesebb formája. Az ötödik a kulcskérdés: „ki vagyok én, hogy akadályozzam Istent?” Ez nem diadal, hanem meghátrálás. Péter nem arról beszél, hogy neki igaza lett, hanem arról, hogy nem volt beleszólása. A hatodik a hallgatóság reakciója, amely rendkívül ritka dolog: elhallgatnak, majd dicsőítik Istent. Nem azt mondják, hogy „megfontoljuk”, és nem is azt, hogy „ez kivételes eset volt”. Egy egész közösség mond le arról, amit addig biztosan tudott. A hetedik a megfogalmazás: „a pogányoknak is megadta Isten a megtérést.” Alany: Isten. Ők nem engedélyt adnak, hanem tudomásul vesznek. A különbség óriási: az egyik fölényt feltételez, a másik felismerést. A nyolcadik, amiért ez a rész fontos a könyv egészében: a következő fejezetekben ez a kérdés újra és újra vissza fog térni, és a 15. fejezetben egy egész tanácskozás foglalkozik vele. Vagyis a vita nem ért véget itt. Egy közösség nem egyetlen beszélgetés alatt változik meg — de valahol el kell kezdődnie, és itt kezdődött el.

verse.text: Ki vagyok én, hogy akadályozzam Istent?

e.q: Mit hallottak meg Jeruzsálemben?
e.qe: What did they hear in Jerusalem?
o: Hogy a pogányok is befogadták Isten igéjét
oe: That Gentiles too received God’s word

v.t: Meghallották, hogy a pogányok is befogadták Isten igéjét.

ve.t: They heard that Gentiles too had received God’s word.

e.q: Hogyan fogadták Pétert, amikor visszaért?
e.qe: How was Peter received when he returned?
oe: They began to argue with him

v.t: Amikor Péter Jeruzsálembe ment, vitatkozni kezdtek vele.

ve.t: When Peter went to Jerusalem, they argued with him.

e.q: Mi volt a vád Péter ellen?
e.qe: What was the charge against Peter?
o: Hogy pogányokhoz ment be, és együtt evett velük
oe: He went in to Gentiles and ate with them

v.t: Pogány emberekhez mentél be, és együtt ettél velük.

ve.t: You went in to Gentiles and ate with them.

e.q: Hogyan válaszolt Péter?
e.qe: How did Peter answer?
oe: He told what happened, in order

v.t: Péter belefogott, és sorjában elbeszélte nekik az egészet.

ve.t: Peter began and told them the whole thing in order.

e.q: Mit mondott el Péter a saját reakciójáról?
e.qe: What did Peter say about his own reaction?
o: Hogy ő is azt felelte: semmiképpen sem, Uram
oe: That he too said: by no means, Lord

v.t: Semmiképpen sem, Uram – feleltem én is.

ve.t: “By no means, Lord,” I too replied.

e.q: Kik voltak a tanúi Péter beszámolójának?
e.qe: Who were the witnesses to Peter’s account?
oe: Six brothers who went with him

v.t: Velem jött ez a hat testvér is.

ve.t: These six brothers came with me too.

e.q: Mi történt, amikor Péter beszélni kezdett a házban?
e.qe: What happened when Peter began to speak?
oe: The Holy Spirit came down on them

v.t: Amikor beszélni kezdtem, leszállt rájuk a Szentlélek.

ve.t: As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit came down on them.

e.q: Mit kérdezett Péter a beszéde végén?
e.qe: What did Peter ask at the end of his speech?
oe: “Who was I to stand in God’s way?”

v.t: Ki vagyok én, hogy akadályozzam Istent?

ve.t: Who was I to stand in God’s way?

e.q: Hogyan reagáltak a hallgatók?
e.qe: How did the hearers react?

v.t: Amikor ezt hallották, megnyugodtak, és dicsőítették Istent.

ve.t: When they heard this, they quietened and praised God.

e.q: Mit mondtak ki a végén?
e.qe: What did they say at the end?
o: Hogy a pogányoknak is megadta Isten a megtérést
oe: God gave the Gentiles repentance too

v.t: A pogányoknak is megadta Isten a megtérést az életre.

ve.t: God has given even the Gentiles repentance to life.

m.q: Hol kapta Péter a látomást?
m.qe: Where did Peter receive the vision?

v.t: Joppéban imádkoztam, és révületben látomást láttam.

ve.t: I was praying in Joppa and in a trance saw a vision.

m.q: Mit mondott a hang a látomásban?
m.qe: What did the voice say in the vision?
o: Amit Isten megtisztított, ne mondd tisztátalannak
oe: Do not call unclean what God cleansed

v.t: Amit Isten megtisztított, azt te ne mondd tisztátalannak.

ve.t: What God has made clean, do not call unclean.

m.q: Hányszor történt meg a látomás?
m.qe: How many times did the vision occur?

v.t: Ez háromszor történt meg, majd minden felemelkedett.

ve.t: This happened three times, then all was drawn up.

m.q: Mit mondott a Lélek Péternek?
m.qe: What did the Spirit tell Peter?
o: Menj el velük, semmit ne tétovázz
oe: Go with them, do not hesitate

v.t: A Lélek azt mondta: menj el velük, semmit ne tétovázz.

ve.t: The Spirit said: go with them, do not hesitate.

m.q: Mihez hasonlította Péter a történteket?
m.qe: To what did Peter compare what happened?
o: Ahhoz, ami velük történt a kezdetben
oe: To what happened to them at the beginning

v.t: Ugyanúgy, ahogy ránk is a kezdetben.

ve.t: Just as on us at the beginning.

m.q: Milyen ajándékot kaptak a pogányok Péter szerint?
m.qe: What gift did the Gentiles receive, per Peter?

v.t: Ugyanazt az ajándékot adta nekik, mint nekünk.

ve.t: He gave them the same gift as he gave us.

m.q: Mikor szállt le rájuk a Lélek „a kezdetben”?
m.qe: When did the Spirit come on them “at the beginning”?

v.t: A kezdetben pünkösdkor szállt le rájuk a Lélek.

ve.t: At the beginning the Spirit came on them at Pentecost.

m.q: Mit mondott Péter korábban Cezáreában?
m.qe: What had Peter said earlier in Caesarea?

v.t: Péter korábban kimondta: Isten nem személyválogató.

ve.t: Peter had said: God shows no favouritism.

m.q: Lezárult-e itt a kérdés a könyvben?
m.qe: Was the question settled here in the book?
o: Nem: a 15. fejezetben egy egész tanácskozás foglalkozik vele
oe: No: a whole council deals with it in chapter 15

v.t: A 15. fejezetben egy egész tanácskozás foglalkozik ezzel.

ve.t: In chapter 15 a whole council deals with this.

m.q: Mi volt a kifogás valódi tárgya?
m.qe: What was the objection really about?
o: Az asztal: hogy együtt evett velük
oe: The table: that he ate with them

v.t: A kifogás nem a tanításról szólt, hanem az asztalról.

ve.t: The objection was not about teaching but about the table.

h.q: Miért éppen az étkezés volt a vád tárgya?
h.qe: Why was eating the object of the charge?
o: Az asztal volt a valódi határ, ahol a két világ összeért
oe: The table was the real boundary between the two worlds

v.t: Pogány emberekhez mentél be, és együtt ettél velük.

ve.t: You went in to Gentiles and ate with them.

h.q: Mit NEM tesz Péter a védekezésében?
h.qe: What does Peter NOT do in his defence?
o: Nem hivatkozik a tekintélyére, és nem érvel elvekkel
oe: He does not use his authority or argue principles
He does not tell the truth

v.t: Péter belefogott, és sorjában elbeszélte nekik az egészet.

ve.t: Peter began and told them the whole thing in order.

h.q: Miért említi Péter a hat testvért?
h.qe: Why does Peter mention the six brothers?
oe: It makes what he says checkable

v.t: Velem jött ez a hat testvér is.

ve.t: These six brothers came with me too.

h.q: Miért kezdi Péter a saját tiltakozásával?
h.qe: Why does Peter begin with his own refusal?
o: Így nem föléjük kerül, hanem melléjük: én is ezt gondoltam
oe: It places him beside them, not above: I thought so too

v.t: Semmiképpen sem, Uram – feleltem én is.

ve.t: “By no means, Lord,” I too replied.

h.q: Milyen mondat a „ki vagyok én, hogy akadályozzam Istent?”
h.qe: What kind of sentence is “who was I to stand in God’s way?”
oe: Not a triumph but a retreat

v.t: Ki vagyok én, hogy akadályozzam Istent?

ve.t: Who was I to stand in God’s way?

h.q: Mitől rendkívül ritka a hallgatóság reakciója?
h.qe: What makes the hearers’ reaction so rare?
o: Egy egész közösség lemond arról, amit addig biztosan tudott
oe: A whole community gives up a certainty

v.t: Amikor ezt hallották, megnyugodtak, és dicsőítették Istent.

ve.t: When they heard this, they quietened and praised God.

h.q: Mi a különbség az engedmény és a felismerés között itt?
h.qe: What is the difference between concession and recognition here?
o: Nem engedélyt adnak: tudomásul veszik, hogy Isten adta
oe: They grant no permission: they acknowledge God gave it

v.t: A pogányoknak is megadta Isten a megtérést az életre.

ve.t: God has given even the Gentiles repentance to life.

h.q: Mit tanít, hogy a kérdés később újra visszatér?
h.qe: What does the question returning later teach?
o: Egy közösség nem egyetlen beszélgetés alatt változik meg
oe: A community does not change in one conversation

v.t: A 15. fejezetben egy egész tanácskozás foglalkozik ezzel.

ve.t: In chapter 15 a whole council deals with this.

h.q: Miért ismétli meg a könyv az egész történetet?
h.qe: Why does the book repeat the whole story?
o: Mert a megismétlés maga a lényeg: így lesz közös tudás
oe: The retelling is the point: it becomes shared knowledge

v.t: Péter belefogott, és sorjában elbeszélte nekik az egészet.

ve.t: Peter began and told them the whole thing in order.

h.q: Mit mutat, hogy az együtt étkezés később is kérdés marad?
h.qe: What does eating together remaining a question show?
o: A gyakorlat nehezebben változik, mint a vélemény
oe: Practice changes more slowly than opinion

v.t: Később is visszatérő kérdés lesz, kivel szabad együtt enni.

ve.t: Whom one may eat with will remain a recurring question.

e.q: Jeruzsálemben meghallották, hogy a pogányok is befogadták az igét.
e.qe: Jerusalem heard that Gentiles too received the word.

v.t: Meghallották, hogy a pogányok is befogadták Isten igéjét.

ve.t: They heard that Gentiles too had received God’s word.

e.q: Pétert ünnepléssel fogadták Jeruzsálemben.
e.qe: Peter was welcomed with celebration in Jerusalem.

v.t: Amikor Péter Jeruzsálembe ment, vitatkozni kezdtek vele.

ve.t: When Peter went to Jerusalem, they argued with him.

e.q: A vád az volt, hogy pogányokkal evett együtt.
e.qe: The charge was that he ate with Gentiles.

v.t: Pogány emberekhez mentél be, és együtt ettél velük.

ve.t: You went in to Gentiles and ate with them.

e.q: Péter sorjában elbeszélte, mi történt.
e.qe: Peter told what had happened, in order.

v.t: Péter belefogott, és sorjában elbeszélte nekik az egészet.

ve.t: Peter began and told them the whole thing in order.

e.q: Péter elhallgatta, hogy ő maga is tiltakozott.
e.qe: Peter hid the fact that he too had refused.

story.e: The news reached Jerusalem faster than Peter did. The apostles and the brothers in Judea heard that the Gentiles too had received God’s word. And when Peter came back, they did not congratulate him. They challenged him: “You went in to uncircumcised men and ate with them!” It is worth stopping here. They did not object to the teaching, nor to his speaking about Jesus. It was the eating. That he sat down at their table. Because that was the point where the two worlds actually met, and where the boundary was most visible. And Peter did not argue, nor did he defend himself with principles. He began to tell them, step by step, what had happened. He told them of the vision of the sheet, the voice, his own refusal, the threefold repetition. He told them the messengers arrived just then and that the Spirit said: go with them, do not hesitate. He told them six men had gone with him — that is, there are witnesses. And he told them the main thing: when he began to speak, the Holy Spirit came down on them, just as on us at the beginning. Then he added the sentence that is the heart of this part: “If then God gave them the same gift as he gave us who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I to stand in God’s way?” So Peter does not say that he was right. He says: I could not prevent it, and I would have had no right to. When they heard this, they fell silent. Then they began to praise God and said: “So God has given even the Gentiles the repentance that leads to life.” These few sentences are one of the loveliest scenes in the Bible. A community that had been certain of something all its life listens to an account — and changes its mind. Not because it lost an argument, but because something happened that could not be explained any other way. And notice the words too: they do not say “all right, we will make an exception”. They say God gave it to them as well. They are not granting a concession; they are recognising something.
story.m: The news reached Jerusalem faster than Peter did. The apostles and the brothers living in Judea heard that the Gentiles too had received God’s word. And when Peter went up to Jerusalem, they did not congratulate him: those of the circumcision began to argue with him. The charge ran: “You went in to uncircumcised men and ate with them.” It is worth pausing at that sentence, because it shows exactly where the boundary lay. They did not object that Peter had told them about Jesus, nor that he had baptised them. It was the eating. That he sat at a Gentile’s table and ate from it. The table was the place where the two worlds actually met, and where crossing was hardest. But Peter did not argue and did not defend himself with principles. He began and told them the whole thing in order. He told them he was praying in Joppa and in a trance saw a vision: a vessel like a great sheet came down, lowered by its four corners, full of four-footed animals, wild beasts, reptiles and birds. He told them he heard a voice: “Get up, Peter, kill and eat!” And that he answered: “By no means, Lord, for nothing unholy or unclean has ever entered my mouth.” He told them the voice spoke a second time: “What God has made clean, do not call unclean!” And that this happened three times, after which everything was drawn up into heaven. He told them that at that very moment three men arrived from Caesarea, and that the Spirit told him to go with them and not hesitate. He added that six brothers went with him — so he is not telling it alone, but with witnesses. Then he told what happened in the house: Cornelius related his own vision, and when Peter began to speak, the Holy Spirit came down on them, just as on us at the beginning. And then he said what is the heart of this part: “If then God gave them the same gift as he gave us who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I to stand in God’s way?” So Peter does not claim that he was right. He says: I could not prevent it, and I would have had no right to. When they heard all this, they quietened down and praised God with these words: “So God has given even the Gentiles the repentance that leads to life.” These few sentences are one of the loveliest scenes in the Bible. A community that had been certain of something all its life listens to an account — and changes its mind. Not because it lost an argument, but because something happened that could not be explained any other way. And it is worth noting their words: they do not say “all right, let us make an exception”. They say God gave it to them too. They are not granting a concession; they are recognising something that has already happened.
story.h: On a first reading this part is a repetition: Peter tells again what we read in the previous chapter. But the retelling is the point. Let us look at eight things. The first is the exact wording of the charge. The objection is not that Peter taught Gentiles, nor that he baptised them. “You ate with them.” The table was the real boundary. It is easier to accept someone in principle than to sit down and eat beside them; the book knows exactly which is harder. The second is what Peter does not do. He does not appeal to his authority, though he could: he is first among the Twelve. He quotes no scripture and argues no principles. He tells what happened. The third is the mention of witnesses. “These six brothers came with me too.” Peter does not build on his own experience but on something others also saw. That sentence makes the account checkable, and that is why it is there. The fourth is the order Peter follows: he begins with his own refusal. He tells them that he too said no — twice, in fact. With this he does not place himself above his hearers but beside them: I thought exactly the same. That is one of the oldest and most honest forms of persuasion. The fifth is the key question: “who was I to stand in God’s way?” That is not a triumph but a retreat. Peter does not speak of being proved right but of having had no say. The sixth is the hearers’ reaction, which is an extremely rare thing: they fall silent, then praise God. They do not say “we will consider it”, nor “this was an exceptional case”. A whole community gives up something it had been certain of. The seventh is the wording: “God has given even the Gentiles repentance.” The subject is God. They are not granting permission; they are acknowledging. The difference is enormous: one presumes superiority, the other is recognition. The eighth is why this part matters to the whole book: in the following chapters this question will return again and again, and in chapter 15 an entire council will deal with it. So the debate did not end here. A community does not change in a single conversation — but it has to begin somewhere, and here it began.

verse.text: Who was I to stand in God’s way?
